one_liner: AES-round Rust hash: about 1.5-2.35x XXH3's bulk throughput in SMHasher suites, but slower than XXH3 on keys under 32 bytes.
what_it_does: gxhash is a non-cryptographic, seeded hash for byte slices, written in Rust. It exposes one-shot functions gxhash32/gxhash64/gxhash128(&[u8], i64 seed), a GxHasher/GxBuildHasher pair implementing Hasher/BuildHasher, and gxhash::HashMap/HashSet aliases (the HashMapExt trait supplies new()). Within a major version, output is identical on x86, ARM and the VAES 'hybrid' build. The Hasher-trait path gives different values from the one-shot functions on the same bytes. An in-repo ffi crate builds a cdylib/staticlib exposing gxhash32/gxhash64 to C.
how_it_is_fast: Each 16-byte block is absorbed into a 128-bit SIMD lane with a single keyless AES round (AESENC on x86, AESE+AESMC on ARM). Inputs over 128 bytes run 4, 8 or 16 independent lanes, so the AES units stay busy (instruction-level parallelism), and the lanes are then folded together in a tree. Inputs of 17-128 bytes are read with overlapping unaligned loads from both ends, which avoids masking. Inputs under 16 bytes use one 16-byte load that deliberately reads past the end of the slice when that stays inside the same 4 KiB page (the 'read beyond' trick), with the padding bytes set to the length. The large-input path is kept out of line (inline(never), extern "C" so vectors pass in registers), which keeps the inlined code at each call site small. The optional nightly 'hybrid' feature uses VAES+AVX2 to process two lanes per instruction.
when_to_use: Bulk hashing of buffers from a few hundred bytes up (dedup chunks, content keys, large string keys) on x86-64 with AES-NI or AArch64 with AES. rurban SMHasher has gxhash64 at 48.9 GB/s against 20.9 GB/s for xxh3 on a Ryzen 5 3350G.

Rust applications (not libraries) built with target-cpu=native whose HashMap keys are mostly strings. In rapidhash's hash-table suite (target-cpu=native), gxhash beats foldhash-f on AMD EPYC 9R14 (geomean 5.01 vs 5.24) and Xeon 8488C (4.73 vs 4.88), and rapidhash's notes call it 'a great choice' for AES-guaranteed, string-heavy use.
When you need a 128-bit hash at 64-bit cost: gxhash128 has the same construction and cost as gxhash64.
Mixed x86/ARM fleets that need the same hash value on both (the stability tests cover aarch64, x86_64 and x86_64-hybrid), as long as everyone stays on one major version.
when_not_to_use: Workloads dominated by short keys (under about 32 bytes). SMHasher3 has gxhash-64 at 37.35 avg cycles for 1-32 bytes against 30.69 for XXH3-64, and rurban has 36.61 cycles/hash against 29.46 for xxh3 and 22.04 for rapidhash.

Libraries, portable binaries, WASM or CPUs without AES. Without aes+sse2 (x86) or aes+neon (ARM) it is a compile_error; there is no fallback (issue #47, open since 2023), no WASM support (#7, open), and no runtime CPU detection.

Tables keyed by attacker-controlled input. The released 3.x line (crates.io 3.5.0) has seed-independent multicollisions (#83, still open): explicit 24-byte and 15-vs-16-byte colliding pairs were posted 2026-09-18. The 4.0 rewrite says it fixes this, but it was merged 2026-09-26, is not on crates.io, and has no independent analysis yet.

Safety-critical code, or code that must run clean under Miri. The README says the crate is not intended for safety-critical use. Miri reported UB on keys shorter than 16 bytes in 3.5.0 (#123, closed as intended), and #111 (open) reports a panic under debug-assertions in release builds on Apple Silicon.

Quality-sensitive uses such as sketches or MinHash. The SMHasher3 port of 3.x passes 226/250 tests, failing Sparse, TwoBytes, SeedZeroes, SeedSparse and Seed; rurban's table flags it 'oob UB, AES only'.

integration.dependencies: rustversion 1.0 (compile-time proc macro; the README nevertheless advertises 0 dependencies); std optional (default feature)
integration.min_toolchain: Not declared (Cargo.toml has no rust-version). CI builds on Rust 1.65, 1.72 and 1.78. The hybrid feature requires nightly (feature(stdarch_x86_avx512)).
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 with AES-NI+SSE2 (uses SSSE3 when enabled); ARM/AArch64 with AES+NEON; hybrid needs x86-64 VAES+AVX2 on nightly. Any other target fails to compile.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. GxHasher and GxBuildHasher are Clone value types holding one 128-bit vector, with no global or shared mutable state; GxBuildHasher::default takes its randomness from std's RandomState.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is a drop-in BuildHasher for std HashMap/HashSet. It does not replace XXH3 as a content hash: the output differs, there is no XXH3-style streaming state for bytes (GxHasher::write chains per call, so chunking changes the value), and C access is only through the unpublished in-repo ffi crate.

gotchas: Version skew: GitHub main is 4.0.0, merged 2026-09-26 with a new construction and new hash values, but crates.io still serves 3.5.0 (2025-03-11). The independent SMHasher/SMHasher3 numbers and the published collision pairs all concern 3.x.

The repo's .cargo/config.toml (target-cpu=native) applies only inside the repo. Dependents must set RUSTFLAGS themselves (-C target-feature=+aes,+sse2 or target-cpu=native), and native builds can SIGILL on older CPUs (closed #66 was a SIGILL report).

For inputs under 16 bytes it reads up to 15 bytes past the end of the slice (page-checked, now via inline asm so Miri no longer sees it). Tools that audit memory reads, and code with guard-page tricks, should know this.

Hashing through the Hasher trait gives different values from gxhash64/gxhash128 on the same bytes. Enabling the 'deterministic' feature anywhere in the dependency graph (Cargo unifies features) fixes GxBuildHasher's seed at 42 for every map.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick gxhash over xxHash (XXH3), wyhash or aHash when you are in Rust, can guarantee AES hardware, and mostly hash inputs of a few hundred bytes or more. There it is about 2.2-2.35x xxh3 and wyhash and about 5x ahash64 in rurban's bulk column. Prefer rapidhash or foldhash for libraries, portable builds and small-key or integer-heavy hash tables: rapidhash-f leads its native hash-table geomeans (e.g. 4.46 vs 4.73 on Xeon 8488C), and plain rapidhash passes all SMHasher3 tests.
verified_claims_summary: Independent suites tested the 3.x algorithm; neither states compiler or flags. rurban SMHasher on a Ryzen 5 3350G measured gxhash64 at 48,920 MiB/s bulk against 20,854 MiB/s for C xxh3 (about 2.35x), but 36.61 vs 29.46 cycles/hash on small keys. SMHasher3 (hardware not stated in its summary) measured 19.14 vs 12.82 bytes/cycle for XXH3-64 (about 1.5x) and 37.35 vs 30.69 cycles on 1-32 byte keys. The first-party chart (BuildJet 2-vCPU x86_64, last regenerated 2025-05-18) is against the pure-Rust twox-hash 1.6.3 XXH3 port. Read from pixels, it shows roughly 2.6-3.3x at 4-128 B and 5-7x from 256 B to 32 KiB, and on the same chart T1ha0 roughly ties gxhash above 4 KiB.
status_note: Actively maintained by one author: the 4.0 rewrite (claimed 1.02-1.35x faster than 3.5.0 on an M5 Pro) landed on main 2026-09-26 but is not yet released. 3.5.0 has about 1.33M crates.io downloads; MIT-licensed, and the source is about 1,300 lines including tests, small enough to vendor, but 17 issues are open, including the DoS report #83.
